title: Sort Colors
description:
`nums` contains only the values `0`, `1` and `2`, representing red, white and blue. Sort it **in place** so all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s.

Do not call a library sort. The goal is a single pass with constant extra space.
hints: Counting sort works in two passes: count the 0s, 1s and 2s, then overwrite the array. Can you do it in one pass?
Maintain three regions: 0s at the front (ending at `low`), 2s at the back (starting at `high`), and unknowns in between scanned by `mid`.
On a 0 swap with `low` and advance both; on a 2 swap with `high` and move `high` left but do NOT advance `mid`, since the swapped-in value is unexamined; on a 1 just advance `mid`.
approach:
**Dutch National Flag (three-way partition).** Keep three pointers: `low` is the end of the 0-region, `high` the start of the 2-region, and `mid` scans the unknown middle. A 0 at `mid` is swapped to `low` (both advance, because what came back from `low` is a 1 or the same 0). A 2 is swapped to `high` and `high` moves left, but `mid` stays put since the value that arrived has not been examined. A 1 is already in the right region.

**Why it works:** the invariants are `nums[:low]` all 0, `nums[low:mid]` all 1, `nums[high+1:]` all 2. Each iteration either advances `mid` or shrinks `high`, so the unknown region `mid..high` shrinks until empty.

**Common mistakes:** advancing `mid` after swapping with `high` (the classic bug, leaves a 0 or 2 unsorted); using `<` instead of `<=` in the loop condition (skips the final element); reaching for counting sort when the interviewer explicitly asks for one pass.

**Interview follow-ups:** Why is the swap with `low` safe to advance `mid` on? (the region `low..mid-1` is all 1s, so the swapped-in value is a 1, or `low == mid`). Generalise to k colours? (counting sort, or repeated partitions; one-pass with k-1 pointers gets unwieldy). Relation to quicksort's 3-way partition (same scheme, with the pivot as the 'middle' value).
